aic:36654.summary: Two faces of a small gold coin are shown side by side: on one, the emperor Basil I and his son Constantine hold a long patriarchal cross between them; on the other, Christ sits frontally on a throne, haloed, blessing and holding the Gospel book, encircled by the Latin legend naming him King of kings. After more than a century of debate over sacred images, the return of Christ to the gold coinage declared the triumph of the icon in the everyday currency of the empire.
facts: The Art Institute of Chicago records the inscription IhS XPS REX REGNANTIUM ('Jesus Christ, King of those who reign') with the enthroned Christ, and bASILIOS ET CONSTANTI AUGG with the imperial pair.
The museum notes that Basil I's coin, with Christ enthroned on its front, was a radical departure from the coinage of the iconoclast emperors, after the Iconoclastic Controversy of about 730–843.
The coin is about 2 cm in diameter and was a gift of Emily Crane Chadbourne (accession 1940.23).
aic:36654.notes: AIC dates it 868–870; Basil I reigned 867–886. Which face is technically obverse follows the museum (Christ on the front).

cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-heavenly-j.summary: The New Jerusalem is drawn as a square city seen from above, its walls laid flat with twelve gates, each holding an apostle beneath a jewel-like disc; within the chequered courtyard stand the Lamb, John and the angel with the measuring rod. The ordered geometry expresses the perfection of the city whose 'light is the Lamb'.
facts: The Morgan Beatus is the work of the painter-scribe Magius (Maius), who is named in a colophon on fol. 293; it is one of the earliest works of the revived Spanish Apocalypse tradition and of so-called Mozarabic art.
The manuscript has 300 leaves of fine parchment and contains, besides Beatus's Commentary, Jerome's Commentary on Daniel.
cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-heavenly-j.notes: Christ appears as the Lamb. Folio 222v is the standard citation for this miniature; the Commons (Google Art Project) file does not state the folio.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-canticle-habakk.summary: In the centre of the heavens the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding sword, bow and arrows among angels, overpowers a demon of pestilence with his spear: 'before him went the pestilence'. Another demon and a horned devil stretch a rope to measure the earth, and below appear the tents of Cushan, the personified deep lifting up its hands, and the fig tree that shall not blossom with the flock cut off from the fold. Habakkuk's vision is turned into a cosmic battle.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-canticle-habakk.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects-situla-of-gotofredo.summary: Around this ivory holy-water bucket runs a series of arches: in one the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child, between two angels, and the others hold the four evangelists writing their Gospels. A dedicatory inscription bands the rim. Made for an imperial ceremony, the situla places the Incarnate Word at the centre of the Gospel witness.
facts: The museum caption states that it was commissioned by Gotofredo, archbishop of Milan and protégé of Otto II, dedicated to the emperor and used in imperial ceremonies.
The V&A cites this 'Milan situla of about 979' as one of only three Ottonian ivory situlae to survive, with the Basilewsky Situla and one in Aachen.

Q1641077.summary: The figurative east face of this perfectly preserved Celtic cross shows, on the shaft just below the head, the Virgin enthroned with the Christ Child, flanked by angels; on the arms appear Cain slaying Abel and the Sacrifice of Isaac, with David killing the lion above the central boss. The Virgin and Child closely recalls those on the Iona crosses and folio 7v of the Book of Kells.
facts: It is often considered the finest surviving Celtic cross in Scotland and was carved from a single block.
The Virgin-and-Child type may echo the Roman Maria Regina imagery of the iconoclast period.
The west face is largely abstract, with snake-and-boss roundels and four lions around the central boss.

feat:book-of-kells-christ-enthroned.summary: In this full-page miniature from the most celebrated of Insular Gospel books, Christ sits frontally beneath an arch, holding the book of the Gospels, framed by dense interlace, angels and a pair of peacocks. The image fuses Mediterranean icon traditions with the spiralling, jewel-like ornament of Insular art, presenting Christ as the eternal Word at the heart of Scripture.
facts: The peacocks flanking Christ's head were an ancient symbol of incorruptibility and resurrection, since their flesh was believed not to decay.
The page stands near the opening of Matthew's Gospel, a few leaves before the manuscript's famous Chi-Rho monogram page.
The book was stolen from Kells in 1007, according to the Annals of Ulster, for the sake of its 'wrought shrine'; it was recovered a few months later, but its golden, jewelled cover was never found.
Presented to Trinity College Dublin in 1661, it has been on public display in the college's Old Library since the 19th century, with the opening on view changed regularly.
